properties.statement:
`add_change_event` TOOK FOUR ROUND-TRIPS TO DISCLOSE FOUR RULES IT KNEW ON THE FIRST CALL, AND THE FIRST OF THOSE RULES HAD ALREADY BEEN 'FIXED' — IN PROSE. dev_storyflow 2026-09-05, recording a merged fix as a ChangeEvent:

  1. `unknown field 'description'` — prose goes in `summary` (every other constructor they used that day takes `description`)
  2. `expected struct AffectedNodeReq` for a bare id string — the error names the struct, not its shape
  3. `unknown change type: "fix"` — lists thirteen legal values (a good error)
  4. `unknown change subject` — `system` or `record` (a good error, but nothing before it said `subject` was an enum)

Their sentence is the finding: 'THE TOOL KNEW ALL FOUR RULES ON THE FIRST CALL AND DISCLOSED THEM ONE PER FAILURE.'

⭐ ROUND-TRIP 1 IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS, BECAUSE IT WAS ALREADY FIXED AND THE FIX DID NOT REACH THEM. `temporal_tools.rs:378`, in the tool's own description: 'THERE IS NO `description` FIELD: reaching for one is the commonest mistake here, and it is refused rather than stored — reported independently by two projects on 2026-08-19.' That sentence has been served since 2026-08-19. On 2026-09-05 a THIRD project made the identical mistake. The instruction exists, and a user who reaches for the tool in the middle of work does not read a 2 KB description first — which `fact:defect-the-served-instructions-put-their-standing-rules-where-a-client-cap-deletes-them` already measured, and which this session's own agent demonstrated by hitting the markup slip five times after reading the warning that morning.

THE MECHANISM, read from the code rather than the report: the request structs carry `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` and the refusal is serde's own generated message — `unknown field X, expected one of A, B, C`. serde deserialization is FAIL-FAST BY DESIGN: it stops at the first violation, so four violations in one call cost four calls. And it knows nothing about WHICH mistake is common, so the one sentence that would have saved the round trip — 'the prose goes in `summary`' — cannot appear in it.

⭐ SO THE FIX WENT TO THE WRONG LEG. `fact:vocabulary-needs-three-legs-and-a-users-project-gets-none-of-it` says a rule reaches a user only through a typed tool, an INSTRUCTION, and a detector. Here the instruction was written and put where nobody standing at the failure reads it. THE REFUSAL IS THE INSTRUCTION SURFACE THAT IS ACTUALLY READ, because it arrives at the exact moment the reader needs it and is short enough to be read whole. A description is read once, if at all, and often cut by a client cap.

WHAT THEY GOT RIGHT AND WHAT TO KEEP: they praise two of the four errors — the ones that enumerate legal values — and their single ask (wish 19) is that all four behave like those two, in one reply. They also observe that `subject: system | record` is 'a genuinely useful distinction (did the WORLD change, or did the GRAPH's record of it?) and nothing in the field name says so', which is the same instruction-placement point at a smaller scale.

NOT ESTABLISHED: how many other constructors carry a commonest-mistake warning in their description that a serde refusal cannot repeat. Only `add_change_event` was examined, because only it was reported. `ProjectModeReq`, `ComponentReq` and the required-fields resolver all have documented traps of the same shape and were not checked.
